newsitem.title: FRANCE: Voter disillusion lies heavy on Algeria's vote.
newsitem.headline: Voter disillusion lies heavy on Algeria's vote.

text.p: Algerian voters who turned out in large numbers in last year's poll to return Liamine Zeroual to power as president seem less enthusiastic to vote on Thursday in a constitutional referendum, analysts said.

Many Algerians, rather than asking questions about the proposed constitution banning Moslem fundamentalists, assailed government ministers at campaign rallies over corruption, political violence and economic hardship.

Algerian analysts and Algiers-based diplomats said the large turn-out of nearly 75 percent in last year's presidential vote could be attributed to voters' perceptions that the election could help to bring changes.
Most Algerians do not believe that the referendum touches them directly, analysts said.

"The campaign failed to arouse voters'...enthusiasm as last year's presidential poll did, in part because people see the draft constitution as a technical process and also because of disillusion among some sectors of the population," said an Algiers-based diplomat.

Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia, government officials and their political backers criss-crossed the country, five times the size of France, to drum up interest in the referendum, but without much success.
The Algerian Liberte newspaper, summing up the voters' mood, said people have turned campaign meetings into lamentations over lack of housing and job, nepotism and bureaucracy.

"What I am interested in at present is having a house...in the desert or even in India," shouted an elderly woman to a government official at the end of his speech extolling the constitutional reforms.
Many Algerians feel the government has failed to deliver on promises to end Islamist guerrilla violence and high inflation.

"People said the insecurity still cripples their lives and the economy. Many fear being outside homes at nightfall even after the authorities lifted the curfew," said an Algerian analyst who declined to be identified.

In 1995 the authorities lifted the night curfew imposed early in 1992, a signal of confidence in its forces fighting a five-year-old Moslem guerrilla campaign in which more than 60,000 people have died.

A bomb exploded at a bus shelter in Berrouaghia, 70 km (45 miles) south of Algiers, killing one person and wounding 13 others on Monday. A car explosion killed five and wounded 19 on Sunday in the garrison town of Blida, south of Algiers.
The latest death toll brought to more than 140 the number of people killed in the four weeks leading to the poll, according to independent Algerian newspapers.
But officials remain optimistic over Algeria's future. They say most people oppose radical Moslem guerrillas and that economic reforms are yielding results.

Algerian officials estimate that the economy will grow by 4.5 to 5.0 percent in 1996. Foreign currency reserves surged to $3.5 billion this year, enabling the country to pay cash for most of its imports.
"Don't forget the years of hell and sacrifices paid to reach such steps of improvement," prime minister Ouyahia told supporters in campaign rallies.
